title: The Garden Party
focus: a girl's first encounter with death across the class line

teacherSummary.text: The wealthy Sheridans prepare a garden party. Laura learns that a young carter from the poor cottages below, Scott, has been killed, and wants to cancel; her mother and sister refuse. After the party, Laura takes a basket of leftovers to the widow and is led to see the dead man, who looks peaceful and beautiful. She apologizes for her hat and, sobbing, tries to tell her brother Laurie what life is.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this story is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “The Garden Party,” how does Mansfield show a girl's first encounter with death across the class line? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the point of view you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In The Garden Party, how does Mansfield develop the idea of a girl's first encounter with death across the class line? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the point of view in the story helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how The Garden Party develops the idea of a girl's first encounter with death across the class line. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of point of view and imagery shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of The Garden Party (where it begins, turns and ends) and its point of view shape the reader's understanding of a girl's first encounter with death across the class line. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what The Garden Party suggests about a girl's first encounter with death across the class line. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the story's point of view and imagery), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Katherine Mansfield uses point of view in The Garden Party to complicate the reader's understanding of a girl's first encounter with death across the class line. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate The Garden Party within its historical and literary context and argue how the story's treatment of a girl's first encounter with death across the class line responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read The Garden Party alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the story's handling of a girl's first encounter with death across the class line follows or bends those conventions, using the point of view as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to The Garden Party and its treatment of a girl's first encounter with death across the class line. State your method, show what it reveals in the story's point of view and imagery, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads The Garden Party as evidence for a larger claim about a girl's first encounter with death across the class line in The Garden Party. Connect close reading of the story to the whole story, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads The Garden Party as a hinge in the story's larger treatment of a girl's first encounter with death across the class line. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on The Garden Party.

satQuestions.passage: And after all the weather was ideal. They could not have had a more perfect day for a garden-party if they had ordered it. Windless, warm, the sky without a cloud. Only the blue was veiled with a haze of light gold, as it is sometimes in early summer. The gardener had been up since dawn, mowing the lawns and sweeping them, until the grass and the dark flat rosettes where the daisy plants had been seemed to shine. As for the roses, you could not help feeling they understood that roses are the only flowers that impress people at garden-parties; the only flowers that everybody is certain of knowing. Hundreds, yes, literally hundreds, had come out in a single night; the green bushes bowed down as though they had been visited by archangels.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Should a happy event go on when something sad happens nearby? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board. Before we start, a content note: Heads-up: this story includes death of a working man; viewing a body.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are eyesore, meaningly, supervise, ripened, crouched. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “They were the greatest possible eyesore, and they had no right to be in that neighbourhood at all.” In this sentence it means: something ugly that spoils a view. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of The Garden Party would have known. Published in 1922 in the Westminster Gazette; Mansfield drew on her childhood in Wellington, New Zealand. Why does this story matter? A modernist story of free indirect discourse and epiphany. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for point of view.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “And after all the weather was ideal.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to a girl's first encounter with death across the class line? I circle “visited”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find point of view, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for point of view.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of point of view. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: And after all the weather was ideal. They could not have had a more perfect day for a garden-party if they had ordered it. Windless, warm, the sky without a cloud. Only the blue was veiled with a haze of light gold, as it is sometimes in early summer. The gardener had been up since dawn, mowing the lawns and sweeping them, until the grass and the dark flat rosettes where the daisy plants had been seemed to shine. As for the roses, you could not help feeling they understood that roses are the only flowers that impress people at garden-parties; the only flowers that everybody is certain of knowing. Hundreds, yes, literally hundreds, had come out in a single night; the green bushes bowed down as though they had been visited by archangels.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Point of view, Imagery, Irony: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; the app shows the level your teacher assigned (for a 9–10 class, the HS Sophomore prompt reads: Analyze how The Garden Party develops the idea of a girl's first encounter with death across the class line. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of point of view and imagery shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions (focus set for the class level): wait time, think-pair-share on DOK 3/4, follow-up probes.
segments.script: Let's talk. We move from what happens to why it matters to whether it's right. After each question I wait before calling on anyone: think first. Our anchor question: How does this story connect to class and privilege? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence, and end by writing one question of your own.

segments.activity: Story quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the story quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this story suggests about a girl's first encounter with death across the class line, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how point of view shapes a girl's first encounter with death across the class line. Tonight, read the next story and add two words to your etymology log.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
